title: Lightweight parser shared-queue experiments (small-request fast path)
content:
Summary:
We ran a targeted investigation into CPU-side overhead for the small-request fast path (single-token-ish requests, <= 128 bytes) to see why p50/p95 tails occasionally spike under modest load (500-2k rps). The hypothesis was that our lightweight JSON+header parser plus shared queue handoff between IO workers and tokenizer workers causes excessive context switches and alloc churn on Python-heavy paths.

Background:
- Symptoms: intermittent p95 spikes to 20-40ms for tiny requests; baseline p50 ~5ms. Spikes correlate with bursty traffic and when autoscaling/worker recycling occurs.
- Stack traces from incidents often show time spent in Python parse/json, PyObject allocation, and pthread_cond_timedwait wakeups.
- Existing fast-path: IO thread (uv/epoll) reads socket -> minimal header parse in C -> enqueues a RequestRef onto a shared MPMC queue implemented in Python extension -> worker thread dequeues and runs tokenizer (Python + FFI) -> dispatch.

Observations from sampling & perf runs (test bed: c6i.4xlarge-ish local replica):
- Perf + py-spy sampling on steady 1k rps: 60% cycles in C parsing and queue ops, 25% in Python object allocation, 10% in tokenizer hot loops, rest syscalls.
- When turning on low-latency timers (1ms wake window), context switch rate increased 3x and p95 grew by ~12ms.
- eBPF traces show bursts of futex/wake calls right before spike windows.
- Allocator noise: jemalloc stats show small-alloc churn spikes aligning with latency tails.
- Microbench: single-thread JSON parse harness (C) is <0.5ms for typical headers; Python wrapper adds ~0.8-1.2ms for object boxing and GC interaction.

Hypotheses:
1) Shared queue handoff implemented with blocking Python primitives (condition vars) causes wake contention under bursts; worker threads wake frequently and compete, paying OS wake/sched overhead.
2) Boxing of parsed header into Python dict per-request is expensive; we can instead pass an opaque C struct until tokenization to avoid PyObject allocations.
3) Tokenizer startup (creating Python tokenizer objects and tokenizer state) contributes non-negligible overhead; reusing tokenizer state per-worker or preallocating could reduce p50/p95.
4) jemalloc per-thread arenas + small object churn leads to cross-thread fragmentation and occasional stalls during arena maintenance.

Experiments run (commands included):
- Baseline: current main branch. Workload: synthetic small-request generator (random short prompts) at 500/1000/2000 rps for 10m windows.
- Experiment A: Replace Python conditionvar-based queue with C lock-free MPSC queue (FFI). Code: perf/bench/queue_a. Ran 3x 10m windows.
  - Observed: context-switch rate -40%, p95 improved from 26ms -> 14ms at 1k rps. p50 unchanged (~5ms).
- Experiment B: Keep queue, but change header parse wrapper to return a thin C struct pointer (PyCapsule) instead of constructing dict.
  - Observed: p50 reduced by ~0.9ms; p95 reduced by ~2-3ms. Memory alloc rate down ~18%.
- Experiment C: Pre-warm tokenizer objects per-worker (object pool) to avoid per-request construction.
  - Observed: p50 down by ~0.6ms; p99 tail improved for sustained high-load runs.
- Experiment D: Force jemalloc retain -> system to reduce arena churn (environment variable tweak).
  - Observed: minor improvement in tail; not reliable across kernels.

Representative perf commands used: 
- perf record -F 99 -g -- python -m bench.run_small_requests --rps 1000 --duration 600
- sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:sched:sched_wakeup /comm=="python"/ { printf("wakeup %d
", pid); }'
- py-spy record -o flame.svg -- python server.py --config small-path

Key flamegraph notes:
- Baseline flame: big wedge at parse_wrapper -> PyDict_New -> PyObject_Malloc -> tokenizer_setup.
- Queue-A flame: remove PyDict wedge, stack compacts: more cycles in tokenizer inner loop (C FFI) which is desired.

Conclusions so far:
- The biggest single-win for small-request latency was replacing the blocking Python-based queue with a C-side MPSC queue and avoiding per-request Python dict allocation. That change reduced OS wakeups and allocator churn.
- Reusing tokenizer objects further reduces variance but yields diminishing returns after queue and allocation changes.
- Jemalloc tuning can help but is brittle; better approach is to reduce allocations rather than rely on allocator knobs.

Follow-ups / action plan:
1) Land queue change (Experiment A) behind a feature flag for canary rollout. PR referenced in linked_artifacts. Need to add thorough stress tests. Owner: Maya. ETA: 2 weeks.
2) Land header wrapper change (Experiment B) to return PyCapsule+pointer; audit for ownership and lifecycle. Owner: Ravi. ETA: 1 week.
3) Implement per-worker tokenizer pool with bounded size, configurable via env. Owner: Elena. ETA: 3 weeks.
4) Add targeted e2e load tests in CI that exercise small-request fast path at 2k rps for 15m windows and collect p50/p95/p99. Owner: SRE. ETA: coordinate with eng-sre.
5) Long-term: consider moving more of the small-request fast path into a thin C runtime (parser + queue + tokenization entry) to minimize Python transitions; evaluate maintenance and safety tradeoffs.

Open questions / risks:
- Ownership lifecycle for PyCapsule pointers across worker pools (must ensure proper free semantics)
- Debuggability trade-off: moving to C queue reduces Python-level observability; need to add tracing hooks.
- Effects on dedicated/different kernels (arm64) not fully measured; must validate across infra matrix.
- Edge-case handling for malformed headers when using opaque C structs: ensure graceful fallbacks.

Appendix - Quick diffs and workload generator notes:
- queue_a: perf/bench/queue_a has ~450 LOC C lock-free ring + Python cffi shim. Feature-flag: RUNTIME_USE_CQUEUE.
- header_capsule: perf/bench/header_capsule branch replaces make_header_dict with make_header_capsule, adds ownership tests.
- workload generator: bench/tools/small_gen.py supports --burstiness and --payload-size; used seeds 42/43 for reproducibility.

Raw artifacts (attached to PR): flamegraphs, bpftrace captures, jemalloc stats (csv) in PR artifact bundle.

Notes to reviewer:
- Focus review on memory ownership correctness (capsule free) and queue edgecases (overrun behavior).
- If we land queue change, plan a canary where only 10% of traffic hits the new code and collect tail latency + heap profiles for 24 hours.
